prompt: How does an `io.Reader` say the data has ended?
hint: Look at the last line `reader.go` printed.

choices.text: It returns `n` equal to `-1`
choices.why: `n` is never negative; the contract says 0 <= n <= len(p).

choices.text: It returns the error `io.EOF`
choices.why: Right: the end of the data is reported as an error value.

choices.text: It returns a `nil` slice
choices.why: `Read` fills a slice the caller owns; it returns only a count and an error.

choices.text: It panics with a message saying the stream is finished
choices.why: Ending is ordinary, so it is an ordinary return value.

prompt: `reader.go` read 30 bytes eight at a time. Why does it print `buf[:n]` and not `buf`?
hint: What was in the last two bytes of `buf` after the fourth call?

choices.text: `buf` is unexported and cannot be printed
choices.why: A local variable prints fine. The issue is what it holds.

choices.text: Past `n`, `buf` still holds bytes from an earlier call
choices.why: Right: after the fourth call the last two bytes were still `al`.

choices.text: Printing `buf` would consume the reader
choices.why: Printing a slice reads memory, not the Reader.

choices.text: `%q` cannot quote a slice of a fixed size
choices.why: `%q` quotes any `[]byte`; `buf[:n]` is also a slice.

prompt: A loop calls `r.Read(buf)` and does `if err == io.EOF { break }` before using `buf[:n]`. With the `alphabet` Reader, what is lost?
hint: The last call returned data and an error together.

choices.text: Nothing: `EOF` always comes with `n` equal to 0
choices.why: That is what `strings.Reader` did. The contract also allows data and `EOF` in one call, and `alphabet` does it.

choices.text: The first ten letters
choices.why: The first two calls returned `nil` errors, so the loop used them.

choices.text: The last six letters, `uvwxyz`
choices.why: Right. Use the `n` bytes first, then look at `err`.

choices.text: The whole alphabet, because the loop never starts
choices.why: The loop runs; only the call that brings `EOF` is mishandled.

prompt: `io.ReadAll(&alphabet{})` returned the letters and a `nil` error, though the Reader returned `io.EOF`. Why?

choices.text: `alphabet` returned `EOF` only for small buffers
choices.why: It returns `EOF` whenever it runs past `z`, whatever the buffer.

choices.text: Reaching the end is what it was asked to do
choices.why: Right; `ReadAll` and `io.Copy` treat `EOF` as the finish line.

choices.text: `ReadAll` ignores every error from the Reader
choices.why: A real failure, a broken connection say, comes back from `ReadAll` as an error.

choices.text: `fmt` prints `io.EOF` as `<nil>`
choices.why: `reader.go` printed `err=EOF`, so `fmt` shows it.

prompt: An `io.Reader` has exactly one method, called ___.
A Writer's `Write` returns `n` smaller than `len(p)`. What must it also return?
hint: The contract is stricter than Read's on exactly this.

choices.text: Nothing; the caller calls `Write` again with the rest
choices.why: That is the Reader's world. A short write without an error breaks the Writer contract.

choices.text: A non-nil error saying why
choices.why: Right, so a caller can check `err` alone.

choices.text: `io.EOF`, to say the destination is full
choices.why: `EOF` means the end of input; it is not the Writer's word for a full disk.

choices.text: The bytes that were not written
choices.why: `Write` returns a count and an error, nothing else.

prompt: Which of these did `report` write to, unchanged, in `writer.go`? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `os.Stdout`
choices.why: Yes, the terminal.

choices.text: a `bytes.Buffer`
choices.why: Yes, 38 bytes kept in memory.

choices.text: a SHA-256 hash
choices.why: Yes, `sha256.New()` returns a Writer.

choices.text: a file on disk
choices.why: Not in this program; files are lesson 18, and they would work just the same.

prompt: The program's hash and `sha256sum` of the same two lines agreed. What does that check establish?
hint: A hash of different bytes would differ.

choices.text: That `crypto/sha256` is faster than the shell
choices.why: Nothing was timed.

choices.text: That the buffer and the terminal received different bytes
choices.why: The opposite: the same function wrote the same bytes to each.

choices.text: `report` wrote exactly those 38 bytes
choices.why: Right; any difference, even a missing newline, changes the hash.

choices.text: That the hash stored the report so it can be read back
choices.why: A hash keeps no copy; what goes in is only digested.

prompt: `counting.go` wrote `one line` and `and another` with `Fprintln`. How many bytes did the counter report?
hint: Count each newline as one byte.

prompt: Two goroutines both write through the same `counter` from `counting.go`. What is wrong?
hint: What does `Write` do to the counter's own field?

choices.text: Nothing, because `os.Stdout` is safe to share
choices.why: The terminal is; `c.n` is not.

choices.text: `c.n += int64(n)` is a data race
choices.why: Right: lesson 1's lost update, which a mutex or an atomic fixes.

choices.text: The lines arrive in alphabetical order
choices.why: Nothing sorts writes; the order is whatever the goroutines did.

choices.text: `Fprintln` refuses a Writer that is not a file
choices.why: It accepted `counter` in the single-goroutine run.

prompt: Match each function from `io` with what it gives back.
hint: Some return a Reader, one returns a Writer, one returns both.

pairs.right: a Reader that stops after n bytes
a Reader that also writes what it reads
a Writer that writes to all of several

right_distractors: a Reader that sorts its input

prompt: Why does `pipe.go` write into the pipe from a separate goroutine?
hint: `io.Pipe` has no buffer, like an unbuffered channel.

choices.text: Only goroutines may hold the writing end
choices.why: Any code may; the problem is waiting.

choices.text: To make the copy run twice as fast
choices.why: Speed is not the point; with one goroutine the program does not finish at all.

choices.text: Each write blocks until somebody reads
choices.why: Right: written from `main`, the first `Fprintf` would wait for a reader that never runs.

choices.text: The race detector requires it
choices.why: The detector has nothing to say either way; the pipe synchronises.

hint: How does the reading side learn the data has ended?

choices.text: `io.Copy` waits for ever after three lines
choices.why: Right: without the close there is no `EOF`, and `main` is left waiting.

choices.text: The hash comes out different
choices.why: The program never reaches the line that prints it.

choices.text: Nothing, because the goroutine ends anyway
choices.why: The goroutine ending does not tell the reader anything; only `Close` does.

choices.text: `io.Copy` returns 69 and an error
choices.why: It does not return at all.

prompt: `go run -race pipe.go` exited 0 with nothing on standard error. Two goroutines handled the same bytes. Why no race?
hint: Section 04 of lesson 16: a value that moves.

choices.text: The detector does not check code in the `io` package
choices.why: It checks the whole program, standard library included.

choices.text: The goroutine ran before `main` started reading
choices.why: It could not: each write waited for a read.

choices.text: The pipe hands each chunk over, so nothing is shared
choices.why: Right, as a channel does.

choices.text: `os.Stdout` was redirected to `/dev/null`
choices.why: The redirect hides the output; it does not change what the goroutines did.

prompt: Order the path one chunk of bytes takes through `pipe.go`.
hint: It starts in the goroutine and ends in two places at once.
items: `io.Copy` reads it from the tee over `pr`
the tee writes it into the hash
the multi-writer writes it to the terminal and `kept`

prompt: A function `CountLines(f *os.File) int` is hard to test. What change does the lesson recommend?
hint: What would a test pass in?

choices.text: Write the test's input to a temporary file first
choices.why: That works, and it is the cost the change avoids.

choices.text: Take an `io.Reader` instead of `*os.File`
choices.why: Right: a file still works, and a test passes a `strings.Reader`.

choices.text: Return a `[]byte` instead of an `int`
choices.why: The result is not what makes it hard to test; the input is.

choices.text: Make it a method on a type that holds the file path
choices.why: Still tied to the disk, just one step further away.

prompt: `reader.go` read a 30-byte string with an 8-byte buffer. How many calls to `Read` did it make, counting the one that returned `EOF`?

hint: The table: one after another, as if concatenated.

choices.text: `abcd`
choices.why: Right: the second Reader starts where the first ends.

choices.text: `ab`, since the first Reader ends with `EOF`
choices.why: MultiReader swallows each inner `EOF` until the last Reader is done.

choices.text: `acbd`, one byte from each in turn
choices.why: That would be interleaving; MultiReader reads them one after another.

choices.text: an error: two Readers cannot share one `EOF`
choices.why: There is one `EOF`, at the end of the last Reader, and `ReadAll` reports no error for it.
